editorial.tagline: The premium travel card that actually pays for itself — if you use the credits.
pros: 8x earning through Chase Travel and Points Boost at 2cpp make portal bookings genuinely valuable
Priority Pass lounge access for you and 2 guests eliminates airport food spending
$300 travel credit applies automatically with zero effort
Primary rental car insurance saves $15-30/day on every rental
Transfer partners (Hyatt, United, Southwest) unlock outsized redemption value
cons: $795 annual fee is steep — you need to actively use credits to come out ahead
Earning rates outside travel and dining are a flat 1x, which is mediocre for everyday spending
StubHub and Peloton credits are niche — worthless if you don't use those services
Chase One Sapphire rule means you can't hold this and the Sapphire Preferred simultaneously
editorial.verdict: The CSR is the best premium travel card for people who actually travel. The $795 fee sounds intimidating, but between the $300 travel credit, lounge access, and Points Boost redemptions, most frequent travelers come out well ahead. Pair it with a Freedom Unlimited for everyday spending and you have a top-tier setup. If you travel fewer than 5 times a year, the Sapphire Preferred is the smarter pick.

editorial.verdict: The CSP is the best entry point into the points and miles world. The 75K bonus is worth nearly $1,000 when transferred to Hyatt, and the $95 fee is a fraction of what premium cards charge. If you eat out regularly and travel a few times a year, this card pays for itself immediately. Graduate to the CSR later when you're ready for the lounge life.

1.5x is good but not spectacular in any single category
Signup bonus is modest (20K points) compared to Sapphire cards
editorial.verdict: The CFU is the backbone card of any Chase portfolio. It won't win headlines, but 1.5x on literally everything — with no annual fee — quietly earns more points than most category cards. Pair it with a Sapphire Preferred or Reserve and every dollar you spend becomes transferable to Hyatt, United, and Southwest. If you're only going to have two Chase cards, make this one of them.

editorial.tagline: The category bonus hunter — 5x rotating categories keep things interesting.
pros: 5x on rotating quarterly categories ($1,500/quarter) can net 30,000+ bonus points per year
3x on dining and drugstores is strong for a no-annual-fee card
Cell phone protection (up to $800/claim) replaces expensive carrier insurance
Points pool with Sapphire cards for transfer partner access
5x on Chase Travel portal purchases
cons: Requires quarterly activation and tracking — easy to forget and miss a whole quarter
$1,500 quarterly cap on 5x categories limits the upside for bigger spenders
Foreign transaction fee (3%) rules it out for international use
1x base rate on non-bonus spending is weak compared to CFU's 1.5x
editorial.verdict: The Freedom Flex is for people who enjoy optimizing. If you'll actually activate quarterly categories and shift spending accordingly, the 5x earning is unbeatable at $0/year. But if you want simplicity, the Freedom Unlimited's flat 1.5x earns more for most people with zero effort. Best strategy: carry both and use each where it's strongest.

editorial.tagline: The ultimate premium card — but only if you'll actually use the avalanche of credits.
pros: Centurion Lounges are genuinely excellent — better food, drinks, and atmosphere than Priority Pass
5x on flights booked directly is the highest airline earning rate from any general-purpose card

cons: $895 annual fee is the highest of any personal card — you need to actively manage credits to justify it

editorial.verdict: The Platinum is the gold standard for frequent travelers who fly 10+ times a year and stay at hotels regularly. The Centurion Lounges alone are worth the card if you connect through hubs like DFW, JFK, or SFO. But be honest with yourself: if you won't use the Resy credits, don't care about Oura, and rarely fly — the Venture X gives you 80% of the experience for less than half the fee.

editorial.tagline: The best card for people who eat — 4x on dining and groceries with credits that actually make sense.
pros: 4x on dining worldwide and US supermarkets is the highest combined food earning rate available
$120 Uber Cash + $120 dining credit + $100 Resy credit + $84 Dunkin' = $424/yr in food-related credits
3x on flights booked directly is strong for a mid-tier card
Transfer partners (ANA, Virgin Atlantic, Delta) unlock premium award flights
Credits are genuinely useful — Uber Eats, restaurants, and groceries are things most people spend on
cons: $325 annual fee has crept up and now requires using most credits to break even
1x on everything outside dining/groceries/flights — no gas, no streaming, no online shopping bonus
Monthly credit cadence ($10/mo Uber, $10/mo dining, $7/mo Dunkin') requires consistent use to capture full value
It's a charge card, not a credit card — balance must be paid in full monthly (Pay Over Time available but not ideal)
Amex acceptance gaps can be frustrating at farmers markets, small shops, and internationally
editorial.verdict: The Amex Gold is the best card for people whose biggest spending categories are restaurants and groceries — and that's most people. The 4x earning rate is unmatched, and unlike the Platinum's niche credits, the Gold's credits (Uber, dining, Dunkin') align with how people actually spend. At $325/year it's not cheap, but if you spend $500+/month on food, the math works easily. The ideal Amex setup is Gold for everyday + Platinum for travel.

editorial.verdict: The Custom Cash is a genius concept: a 5x card that requires zero effort. Slot it into your wallet for one specific category (gas or groceries work best) and stay under $500/month in that category. It's perfect as a specialist card in a larger portfolio. Pair it with a Strata Premier and your ThankYou Points become transferable to airline partners. Don't try to make it your only card — the 1x base rate is too weak.

It's the ultimate backup card and the right default for any spending that doesn't fall into a bonus category on another card. If you're building a Citi setup, pair it with a Strata Premier to turn that 2% into transferable points worth 1.5-2+ cents each.

editorial.verdict: The Venture X is the best value in premium travel cards, full stop. When you factor in the $300 travel credit and anniversary miles, you're paying effectively nothing for lounge access that covers your whole travel group. It's the card I'd recommend to anyone who wants the premium travel experience without the $800+ annual fee of the CSR or Amex Platinum. The only real weakness is the smaller transfer partner ecosystem.

editorial.verdict: The SavorOne is a top-tier no-fee card that earns 3x on the categories that matter most for everyday life. It's the perfect companion to a Venture X — you earn 3x on food and fun, 2x on everything else, and funnel all points into the same transferable pool. Even standalone, 3% back on dining and groceries beats most cash back cards. If you're building a Capital One setup, start here.

The average American renter pays $1,700/month — that's 20,400 Bilt points per year on money you're already spending, transferable 1:1 to Hyatt where they're worth 2+ cents each. That's $400+/year in travel value from rent alone. The 1x rate on other purchases is weak, so use it only for rent and housing payments. Pair with a CSP or Amex Gold for everything else.

editorial.verdict: The IHG Premier is the best hotel card you've never heard of. The 4th-night-free benefit alone can save hundreds on a single vacation, and the annual free night more than covers the fee. IHG has the largest hotel portfolio in the world (Holiday Inn, Kimpton, InterContinental, Crowne Plaza), so chances are there's an IHG property wherever you're going. If you stay at IHG 3+ nights a year, this card is a must-have.

editorial.tagline: The card for Delta loyalists — free bags, priority boarding, and a path to status.

editorial.verdict: The Delta Gold is a straightforward value proposition: if you fly Delta 3+ times a year, the free checked bag alone covers the $150 fee. The priority boarding and inflight savings are nice bonuses. But be honest about whether you're truly a Delta loyalist — if you price-shop airlines, a flexible points card like the CSP or Venture X will serve you better. This card is for people who've already decided Delta is their airline.
